literal: When Zhen became inspector, Qiusheng had once committed an offense; nursing hatred he plotted disloyalty and, falsely under the pretext of marriage, entered the city and told the people: "The inspector wishes to move the great households of the city and send them toward Dai."
idiomatic: When Zhen took office Qiusheng, smarting from an earlier offense, plotted treason; under cover of a wedding he entered the city and told the people, "The inspector means to uproot the leading families and send them to Dai."

literal: Together they plotted to turn the city.
idiomatic: They conspired to seize the city.

literal: The townsman Shi Daoqi secretly reported the affair to Zhen; he swiftly seized Qiusheng and all who shared the plot.
idiomatic: A townsman named Shi Daoqi reported the plot in secret; Zhen moved at once to seize Qiusheng and his fellow conspirators.

literal: Zhen said: "I have not failed others; why should others rebel? Only Qiusheng has deceived and misled them.
idiomatic: Zhen said, "I have wronged no one—why should they rebel? Only Qiusheng has misled them.

literal: If I seize them at once the multitude will surely be greatly afraid.
idiomatic: If I arrest them now the people will panic.

literal: I will wait quietly; before long they will themselves repent and submit."
idiomatic: I will wait calmly; soon they will repent and submit of themselves."

literal: Before the words were finished, three hundred men in the city bound themselves and came to the prefectural gate, stating Qiusheng's crime of deceit and delusion.
idiomatic: He had barely finished speaking when three hundred townsmen came to the gate with ropes on their own backs, denouncing Qiusheng's lies.

literal: Qiusheng fled alone on horseback.
idiomatic: Qiusheng escaped on a lone horse.

literal: Zhen pardoned and did not inquire.
idiomatic: Zhen pardoned him and pursued the matter no further.

literal: Later he was summoned as Director of Pasturage in the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He was later recalled as Director of Pasturage in the Masters of Writing.

literal: He died; posthumously he was made Attendant-in-ordinary and given the same ceremonial rank as the Three Dukes; posthumous title Duke Jian.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Attendant-in-ordinary with the ceremonial rank of the Three Dukes, styled Duke Jian.

literal: He had eight sons.
idiomatic: Eight sons survived him.

literal: The fifth son Rui.
idiomatic: The fifth son was Rui.

literal: At first Rui's mother the Lady Yin, while pregnant, suffered an injury.
idiomatic: Rui's mother Lady Yin had been injured while carrying him.

literal: Later while painting in her chamber she dreamed an old man in full cap and robes told her: "I grant you a son; do not worry."
idiomatic: Later, resting in her chamber, she dreamed an old man in court dress who said, "I give you a son—do not grieve."

literal: When she awoke she rejoiced in private.
idiomatic: She woke and rejoiced in secret.

literal: She again asked a diviner; the diviner said: "Great fortune."
idiomatic: She consulted a diviner, who said, "Great fortune."

literal: Before long Rui was born; Zhen thought it accorded with the dream, and therefore named him Rui, style Tiansi.
idiomatic: Soon after Rui was born; Zhen took it as fulfillment of the dream and named him Rui, style Tiansi.

literal: He held the post of Grand Master of Palace Counsel.
idiomatic: He served as Grand Master of Palace Counsel.

literal: He died; posthumously he was made Minister of Ceremonies.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Minister of Ceremonies.

literal: Yi's younger brother Lie was fierce in martial bearing and had wisdom and stratagem.
idiomatic: Yi's brother Lie was bold in war and shrewd in counsel.

literal: In Yuan Shao's rebellion the hundred officials did not dare speak; only Lie went out, feigned attachment to Shao, and enlisted men to seize Emperor Taizong.
idiomatic: During Yuan Shao's revolt the court was mute; only Lie went abroad, pretended to join Shao, and raised men to seize Emperor Taizong.

literal: Shao trusted him; he himself went out from Yanchiu Gate and then welcomed and established Emperor Taizong.
idiomatic: Shao trusted him; Lie led his men out through Yanchiu Gate and brought Emperor Taizong to the throne.

literal: For merit his title was advanced to Prince of Yinping.
idiomatic: For this service he was raised to Prince of Yinping.

literal: He died; posthumous title Xi.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously styled Xi.

literal: His son Qiu succeeded.
idiomatic: His son Qiu inherited the line.

literal: Lie's younger brother Gu was brave in stratagem and had daring spirit; in youth he followed his elder brother Yi in attending Taizu and guarded left and right.
idiomatic: Lie's brother Gu was bold and resourceful; in youth he followed Yi in serving Taizu as a guardsman.

literal: He was sent to Murong Chui; in Chui's last years government lay with subordinates, and they therefore detained Gu to demand a bribe.
idiomatic: Sent to Murong Chui, he found the court in Chui's last years controlled by underlings who detained him and demanded a bribe.

literal: Taizu broke off relations.
idiomatic: Taizu broke off relations with Yan.

literal: Gu led several tens of horsemen on his left and right, killed their guard general, and fled back.
idiomatic: Gu rode out with a few dozen men, killed the guard commander, and fled home.

literal: He was seized by Murong Bao, returned to Zhongshan, and Chui treated him with ever greater generosity.
idiomatic: Murong Bao captured him and brought him back to Zhongshan, where Chui treated him with growing favor.

literal: Gu thereupon devoted himself to study, recited and read several hundred thousand words of the classics, and Chui's countrymen all praised and valued him.
idiomatic: Gu applied himself to learning, mastered hundreds of thousands of words of the classics, and won esteem throughout Yan.

literal: When Taizu attacked Zhongshan, Murong Pulong had already set himself up and then killed Gu to firm the hearts of the multitude; when Taizu heard of it he grieved bitterly.
idiomatic: When Taizu marched on Zhongshan, Murong Pulong, having seized power, killed Gu to bind his followers to him; Taizu mourned deeply when he heard.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified he opened Pulong's coffin, cut down his corpse, seized Gao Ba, Cheng Tong, and others who had plotted Gu's death, and exterminated all five degrees of kin; he had them killed by hacking with great blades.
idiomatic: After Zhongshan fell he opened Pulong's coffin and hacked the corpse apart, seized Gao Ba, Cheng Tong, and the rest who had plotted Gu's death, exterminated their clans to the fifth degree, and had them cut apart with great blades.

literal: He then reburied Gu, posthumously enfeoffed him Prince of Qin Min, and enfeoffed his son Kui Prince of Yuzhang to continue Gu's line.
idiomatic: He reburied Gu as Prince of Qin Min and enfeoffed his son Kui as Prince of Yuzhang to continue the line.

literal: Prince of Changshan Zun was the son of Zhaocheng's son Shoujiu.
idiomatic: Zun, Prince of Changshan, descended from Zhaocheng through his son Shoujiu.

literal: From youth he was strong and brave and did not bind himself to small proprieties.
idiomatic: From youth he was fierce and free of petty scruple.

literal: In early Taizu he had merit in assisting the founding mandate and was granted the title Duke of Lueyang.
idiomatic: In Taizu's early days he helped establish the realm and was made Duke of Lueyang.

literal: When Murong Bao was defeated he separately led seven hundred horsemen to intercept his line of retreat; thereby there was the victory at Canhe.
idiomatic: When Murong Bao was routed he took seven hundred horsemen to block the retreat and won the victory at Canhe.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified he was appointed Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, added Attendant-in-ordinary, and given charge of Hekou in Bohai.
idiomatic: After Zhongshan fell he became Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Attendant-in-ordinary, and held Hekou in Bohai.

literal: [5] When bandits rose in Boling and Bohai, Zun attacked and pacified them.
idiomatic: [5] When bandits rose in Boling and Bohai he suppressed them.

literal: He was moved to Inspector and enfeoffed Prince of Changshan.
idiomatic: He was made Inspector and enfeoffed Prince of Changshan.

literal: Zun loved wine; in the fourth year of Tiansi, for drunken disorder and breach of propriety toward the Princess of Taiyuan, he was granted death and buried with commoner's rites.
idiomatic: Zun drank heavily; in the fourth year of Tiansi he insulted the Princess of Taiyuan while drunk, was granted death, and was buried with common rites.

literal: His son Su was born of Emperor Taizong's mother's younger sister and was especially favored.
idiomatic: His son Su was born to Emperor Taizong's maternal aunt and was singularly favored.

literal: From youth he was brought within to attend; he repeatedly held eminent office, was granted the title Duke of Shang'an, and was appointed Grand Officer of the Outer Court.
idiomatic: Raised from youth in the inner palace, he rose through high office, was made Duke of Shang'an, and became Grand Officer of the Outer Court.

literal: At the beginning of Shizu he again inherited the title.
idiomatic: At Shizu's accession he inherited the title anew.

literal: When the Xiutu of Yuyuan and others rebelled, Su attacked them, beheaded the chieftain, and moved more than a thousand households to the south of Zhuolu, establishing Pingyuan commandery to settle them.
idiomatic: When the Xiutu of Yuyuan rebelled he crushed them, beheaded their leader, and resettled more than a thousand households south of Zhuolu in the new Pingyuan commandery.

literal: When Tongwan was pacified, because Su had authority to win hearts by awe, he was appointed with staff of authority as Grand General Who Pacifies the West to guard it.
idiomatic: After Tongwan fell his reputation for stern mercy won him appointment as Grand General Who Pacifies the West with full authority to hold the region.

literal: Later he was appointed Grand Officer of the Inner Court.
idiomatic: He was later made Grand Officer of the Inner Court.

literal: When Emperor Gaozong ascended the throne he devoted himself to lenient rule and abolished miscellaneous levies.
idiomatic: At Emperor Gaozong's accession he pursued a policy of leniency and abolished miscellaneous levies.

literal: The responsible officials memorialized that state revenue was insufficient and firmly requested their restoration; only Su said: "Your servant has heard, 'When the people are insufficient, with whom shall the ruler be sufficient?'"
idiomatic: Officials reported the treasury empty and begged to restore the levies; only Su said, "I have heard that when the people lack, the ruler cannot abound."

literal: The emperor approved and followed him.
idiomatic: The emperor approved and held to Su's counsel.

literal: An edict ordered the ministers to discuss fixing the princes' names; Su and Minister of State Lu Li deliberated, saying: "In ancient emperors' and kings' institution of names, the form has five kinds: there is trust, there is righteousness, there is image, there is borrowing, and there is category.
idiomatic: The court was ordered to name the newborn princes; Su and Minister of State Lu Li argued that ancient rulers used five kinds of names: trust, righteousness, image, borrowing, and category.

literal: We humbly consider that Your Majesty stands in a flourishing bright fortune, answers a season of glorious expansion, and has begotten a prince; he should be named by virtue.
idiomatic: They urged that at this flourishing season, when Your Majesty had begotten a prince, the child should receive a name drawn from virtue.

literal: Emperor Gaozong followed them.
idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong agreed.

literal: Su was eminent among the clan kindred and was also old; the emperor each time brought him in and consulted him on governing the state.
idiomatic: Su stood foremost among the clan and was by then aged; the emperor often summoned him to counsel on state affairs.

literal: He firmly declined on grounds of illness and returned to his residence.
idiomatic: He pleaded illness and withdrew to his home.

literal: By nature he was upright and square; in office for fifty years he was the same from first to last; opinion of the time praised him as worthy.
idiomatic: Upright by nature, he served fifty years without change, and his age called him worthy.

literal: He died; posthumous title Kang; he was buried with honor at Jinling and received sacrifice in the temple court.
idiomatic: He died, was styled Kang, buried at Jinling, and honored with temple sacrifice.

literal: His eldest son Kesiling, aged seventeen, followed Shizu on the hunt, met a fierce tiger, and Kesiling then fought it empty-handed and presented it.
idiomatic: His eldest son Kesiling, seventeen, joined Shizu on a hunt, met a tiger, and brought it down bare-handed as tribute.

literal: Shizu said: "Your talent and strength are unmatched; you should establish deeds for the state—do not act thus."
idiomatic: Shizu said, "Your strength is matchless—serve the state with deeds, not with stunts like this."

literal: He was at once appointed Inner Aghan.
idiomatic: He was at once made Inner Aghan.

literal: He again followed in pacifying Liangzhou.
idiomatic: He joined the pacification of Liangzhou.

literal: Juqu Maoqian ordered a fierce general to engage Kesiling; both spears broke.
idiomatic: Juqu Maoqian sent a champion against Kesiling; both spears shattered.

literal: Kesiling drew an arrow and shot him; he fell from his horse; Kesiling feared rescue would arrive, and before he could draw his sword he used a knife to cut across the neck and made body and head separate places.
idiomatic: Kesiling shot him from the saddle; before reinforcements could arrive and before he could draw his sword he slit the man's throat with a knife and severed head from body.

literal: Shizu admired him; that same day he was appointed Chief of the Imperial Banners and enfeoffed Marquis of Jiyang.
idiomatic: Shizu admired the feat and that same day made him Chief of the Imperial Banners and Marquis of Jiyang.

literal: He died while Chief General of the Central Army.
idiomatic: He died in office as Chief General of the Central Army.

literal: His younger brother Peijin succeeded to the title; for an offense the state was abolished.
idiomatic: His brother Peijin inherited the title but lost the fief for a crime.

literal: Peijin's son Zhao, childhood name Ani, was brought in by Zhang Yi of the Masters of Writing as concurrent Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Peijin's son Zhao, called Ani in youth, was introduced by Master of Writing Zhang Yi as a concurrent palace attendant.

literal: When Gaozu was about to observe mourning for Prince of Qi Jun, Zhao instead composed palace music.
idiomatic: When Gaozu was to mourn Prince of Qi Jun, Zhao composed palace music instead.

literal: Gaozu was greatly angered and ordered: "Ani is stupid and dull—who introduced him as attendant!"
idiomatic: Gaozu raged and said, "Ani is a fool—who made him an attendant!"

literal: Thereupon Zhang Yi was demoted to commoner to guard the Masters of Writing, and Zhao was then stopped and dismissed.
idiomatic: Zhang Yi was reduced to commoner rank to serve in the Masters of Writing, and Zhao was dismissed.

literal: In Emperor Shizong's time Zhao's cousin Hui was close in favor and held power; he was gradually promoted to Left Vice Director.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Shizong his cousin Hui held favor and power, and Zhao rose by degrees to Left Vice Director.

literal: When Shizong died Yu Zhong held government; Zhao was Yellow Gate Attendant and again curried favor with him.
idiomatic: After Shizong's death Yu Zhong seized power; Zhao served as Yellow Gate Attendant and fawned on him again.

literal: Zhong monopolized authority and abused power, wrongfully entrapped loyal worthies—many were at Zhao's guidance.
idiomatic: Zhong ruled by force and ruined loyal men, often on Zhao's prompting.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling held court he was Director of the Masters of Writing and Intendant of Henan.
idiomatic: Under Empress Dowager Ling he became Director of the Masters of Writing and Intendant of Henan.

literal: Deaf and obstinate, in handling affairs he was harsh and urgent; wherever he went he was a plague.
idiomatic: Deaf and brutal, he ran affairs with savage haste and was dreaded wherever he served.

literal: Soon he went out as Inspector of Yongzhou; in the province he was greedy and cruel and greatly harmed the people.
idiomatic: He was soon sent out as Inspector of Yongzhou, where his greed and cruelty did great harm.

literal: Later he entered court as Director of the Masters of Writing, fawned on Liu Teng, and was advanced to General Who Pacifies the West.
idiomatic: Recalled to the Masters of Writing, he flattered Liu Teng and was raised to General Who Pacifies the West.

literal: He died; posthumously he was made Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He paid bribes to Yuan Cha, and therefore the posthumous gifts were exceptionally generous.
idiomatic: He had bribed Yuan Cha, and so his funeral honors were lavish.

literal: Zhao's younger brother Shao, style Choulun.
idiomatic: Zhao's brother Shao, style Choulun.

literal: From youth he was clever and keen.
idiomatic: Clever from youth.

literal: He was moved to Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: Shao in judgment did not avoid the strong and overbearing.
idiomatic: In judgment Shao never shrank from the powerful.

literal: Emperor Shizong ordered him to examine Zhao Xiu's prison case; because Xiu was a favorite flatterer, he therefore added cudgel punishment and ordered him to death.
idiomatic: Emperor Shizong ordered him to review Zhao Xiu's case; Xiu was a court favorite, so Shao added beatings and drove the sentence to death.

literal: The emperor reproached Shao for not reporting again.
idiomatic: The emperor rebuked Shao for not seeking a second report.

literal: Shao said: "Xiu's treachery and flattery exceeded Dong Xian's; if your servant did not seize the occasion to remove him, I fear Your Majesty would again bear the name of Emperor Ai."
idiomatic: Shao said, "Xiu's villainy outdid Dong Xian's; had I not seized the chance to remove him, Your Majesty might have gone the way of Emperor Ai."

literal: Because his words were upright, he was therefore not punished.
idiomatic: His words were just, and the emperor spared him.

literal: When he went out, Prince of Guangping Huai bowed to Shao and congratulated him, saying: "Uncle is the integrity of the imperial house—how could Zhu Yun and Ji An even be looked up to in comparison!"
idiomatic: As he left, Prince of Guangping Huai bowed to him and said, "Uncle, you are the house's conscience—Zhu Yun and Ji An are not fit to be named beside you!"

literal: Shao said: "I only regret that the killing was somewhat late; that is my shame."
idiomatic: Shao said, "I only regret the killing came late—that is my shame."

literal: He died while Inspector of Liangzhou.
idiomatic: He died as Inspector of Liangzhou.

literal: Peijin's younger brother Zhong, style Xiande.
idiomatic: Peijin's brother Zhong, style Xiande.

literal: From youth he was deep and steady; he was known for loyalty and prudence.
idiomatic: From youth he was grave and steady, famed for loyalty.

literal: In Gaozu's time he was repeatedly promoted to Right Vice Director, granted the title Duke of Chengyang, added Attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Guards the West; he had merit in assisting and supporting, and the hundred officials all respected him.
idiomatic: Under Gaozu he rose to Right Vice Director, was made Duke of Chengyang, Attendant-in-ordinary, and General Who Guards the West, and won the respect of the whole court for steadfast service.

literal: In the fourth year of Taihe his illness was grave and he declined office; he nursed his illness at Gaoliu.
idiomatic: In the fourth year of Taihe, gravely ill, he resigned and went to nurse his health at Gaoliu.

literal: The imperial carriage personally escorted him beyond the capital gate and granted two hundred bolts of mixed silks; the attending ministers who took leave of him all wept.
idiomatic: The emperor escorted him beyond the capital gate in person, gave him two hundred bolts of silk, and the ministers who bade him farewell wept.

literal: When he died all mourned and regretted him.
idiomatic: At his death the court mourned him.

literal: Posthumous title Xuan; he was ordered to have the responsible officials erect a stele inscription.
idiomatic: He was styled Xuan, and the throne ordered officials to raise a memorial stele.

literal: He had seventeen sons.
idiomatic: He left seventeen sons.
